question: What does 'Gillick competence' assess?
options: Whether a person aged 16 or 17 can refuse treatment
Whether a child under 16 has sufficient understanding and maturity to consent to their own medical treatment without parental knowledge or consent
Whether a parent can consent on behalf of a child
Whether a child can be detained under the Mental Health Act
rationale: Gillick competence assesses whether a child under 16 fully understands what is proposed and has sufficient maturity to consent to their own treatment, following the Gillick ruling and Lord Scarman's test.
source: NSPCC Learning - Gillick competence and Fraser guidelines

question: The Fraser guidelines apply specifically to which area of advice and treatment for under-16s?
options: Admission to hospital under the Mental Health Act
Contraception and sexual health (and, since 2006, sexually transmitted infections and termination of pregnancy)
Detention in police custody
Consent to surgery of any kind
rationale: Fraser guidelines apply specifically to contraception and sexual health advice/treatment; a 2006 ruling extended them to sexually transmitted infections and termination of pregnancy. Gillick competence is the broader concept.
source: NSPCC Learning - Gillick competence and Fraser guidelines

scenario: A 14-year-old asks for contraceptive advice and refuses to tell her parents.
question: Under the Fraser guidelines, which of the following is NOT one of the conditions a practitioner must be satisfied about before providing advice or treatment?
options: The young person cannot be persuaded to inform their parents or allow the practitioner to do so
The young person understands the advice given
The young person has obtained written consent from a person with parental responsibility
The young person's physical or mental health is likely to suffer without the advice or treatment
rationale: The Fraser conditions do not require parental consent - the whole point is that treatment can proceed without it. The conditions concern the young person's understanding, best interests, likely continuation of sexual activity, and risk to health.
source: NSPCC Learning - Gillick competence and Fraser guidelines

question: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, from what age is a young person presumed to have capacity to make their own decisions in the same way as an adult (unless assessed as lacking it)?
rationale: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies to people aged 16 and over, so 16- and 17-year-olds are presumed to have capacity to make decisions unless assessed otherwise.
source: SCIE - Mental Capacity Act 2005 at a glance

scenario: A 17-year-old with capacity refuses informal admission to hospital for treatment of a mental disorder.
question: According to the Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (Chapter 19), can a person with parental responsibility consent to the admission on the young person's behalf?
options: Yes, parental responsibility always overrides a young person's refusal
No - if a 16 or 17 year old with capacity refuses, a person with parental responsibility cannot consent on their behalf to override it
Only if two parents both agree
Only if the young person is under a Care Order
rationale: The Code of Practice states that where a 16-17 year old with capacity refuses informal admission, a person with parental responsibility cannot consent on their behalf; it is inadvisable to rely on parental consent to override a capacitous young person's refusal.
source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice - Chapter 19

question: Under the Children Act 1989, which parent automatically has parental responsibility from birth in England and Wales?
options: The birth mother (unless removed by an adoption or parental order)
The father only
Whichever parent registers the birth first
Both parents only if they are cohabiting
rationale: The birth mother automatically has parental responsibility (unless removed by adoption or a parental order). A married father also has it; an unmarried father acquires it only by birth registration, agreement, or court order.
source: GOV.UK - Parental responsibility (Children Act 1989)

scenario: An unmarried couple have a baby. The father is not yet registered on the birth certificate.
question: Under the Children Act 1989, how can an unmarried father acquire parental responsibility?
options: It happens automatically once the child is born
Only through adoption
By being registered as the child's father on the birth certificate, by a parental responsibility agreement with the mother, or by court order
Only if he later marries the mother
rationale: An unmarried father acquires parental responsibility by jointly registering the birth (being named on the certificate), a parental responsibility agreement with the mother, or a court order.
source: GOV.UK - Parental responsibility (Children Act 1989)

question: Which section of the Mental Health Act 1983 places a duty on hospital managers to ensure patients under 18 are accommodated in an environment suitable for their age?
options: Section 2
Section 117
Section 131A
Section 136
rationale: Section 131A requires hospital managers to ensure that under-18s admitted for mental disorder are accommodated in an environment suitable for their age, subject to their needs.
source: Mental Health Act 1983, Section 131A / Mental Health Law Online

scenario: An under-18 is being considered for admission to an adult psychiatric ward because no CAMHS bed is immediately available.
question: Under section 131A of the Mental Health Act 1983, when determining whether the environment is suitable, whom must hospital managers consult?
options: A police officer
A person with experience in child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) cases
The Care Quality Commission chair
The child's headteacher
rationale: Section 131A requires managers to consult a person they consider suitable because of their experience in CAMHS cases when determining whether the environment is age-suitable.
source: Mental Health Act 1983, Section 131A / Mental Health Law Online

scenario: A 16-year-old is placed on an adult psychiatric ward in exceptional circumstances.
question: A provider must notify the Care Quality Commission (CQC) when a patient under 18 is placed on an adult psychiatric ward for a continuous period longer than how many hours?
options: 24 hours
48 hours
72 hours
1 week
rationale: CQC must be notified when an under-18 is placed on an adult psychiatric ward for a continuous period longer than 48 hours.
source: Care Quality Commission - Children and young people in adult psychiatric units notification

question: Under section 131A, admission of an under-18 to an adult psychiatric ward should occur in what circumstances?
options: Routinely, as adult wards are equally suitable
Only in exceptional circumstances, where it is the most suitable place for that under-18
Only for those aged 17
Never, under any circumstances
rationale: Admissions of under-18s to adult wards are permissible only in exceptional circumstances, where this is judged the most suitable place for the young person.
source: Mental Health Law Online - Age-appropriate accommodation for children (s131A)

question: Under the Children Act 1989, a 'child in need' falls under which section?
options: Section 17
Section 47
Section 20
Section 31
rationale: Section 17 of the Children Act 1989 defines a 'child in need' and places a duty on local authorities to provide services to safeguard and promote their welfare.
source: Children Act 1989, Section 17 / legislation.gov.uk

question: A section 47 enquiry under the Children Act 1989 is triggered when there is reasonable cause to suspect that a child is:
options: Not achieving a reasonable standard of health without services
Suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm
Absent from school
Living in temporary accommodation
rationale: Section 47 places a duty to make enquiries where there is reasonable cause to suspect a child is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm - the child protection threshold, distinct from the 'child in need' (s17) threshold.
source: Children Act 1989, Section 47 / legislation.gov.uk

scenario: A referral raises concerns that a child may be at risk of harm from a caregiver.
question: According to Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023, what is the purpose of a strategy discussion?
options: To arrange respite care for the family
To determine whether the significant harm threshold is met and whether a section 47 enquiry is needed
To decide school placement
To close the case
rationale: A strategy discussion takes place where there is reasonable cause to suspect a child is suffering or likely to suffer significant harm, to determine whether the threshold is met and a section 47 enquiry is required.
source: HM Government - Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023

question: Which distinction did the Children Act 1989 introduce between two categories of concern?
options: Physical harm versus emotional harm
'Child in need' (section 17) versus 'child protection'/significant harm (section 47)
Voluntary versus court-ordered care
Under-5s versus over-5s
rationale: The Children Act 1989 introduced the distinction between 'child in need' (s17, provision of support services) and 'child protection' (s47, investigation of suspected significant harm).
source: Children Act 1989 / legislation.gov.uk

question: Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023 is best described as:
options: Optional best-practice advice
Statutory guidance for multi-agency working to safeguard children
A charity fundraising campaign
Guidance that applies only to schools
rationale: Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023 is the statutory guidance for multi-agency working to safeguard and promote the welfare of children.
source: HM Government - Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023

question: The 'Think Family' approach in safeguarding practice emphasises:
options: Working only with the individual child in isolation
Recognising and responding to the needs of the whole family, including how parental issues affect children and vice versa
Removing children from families as a first response
Focusing solely on financial support
rationale: Think Family promotes coordinated support that considers the whole family - including how adult problems (e.g. parental mental illness) affect children - through joint working and information sharing across services.
source: HM Government - Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023

question: According to NICE guideline NG225 (2022), a child or young person who has self-harmed should receive which key assessment?
options: A numerical risk-prediction score only
A psychosocial assessment by a mental health professional experienced in assessing this group
No assessment if physically well
A blood test only
rationale: NG225 recommends a psychosocial assessment by a mental health professional experienced in assessing children and young people who self-harm.
source: NICE - NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence

scenario: A 15-year-old presents to the ward following an episode of self-harm.
question: According to NICE NG225, what is the guidance on using risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or self-harm repetition?
options: They should be the main basis for decisions
They should not be used to predict future suicide or self-harm repetition or to determine who should receive treatment
They are mandatory for all under-18s
They replace the need for a clinical conversation
rationale: NG225 advises against using risk assessment tools and scales to predict future self-harm or suicide, or to decide who should be offered treatment, favouring a collaborative psychosocial assessment instead.
source: NICE - NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence

question: NICE NG225 states that a psychosocial assessment of a child or young person who has self-harmed should additionally explore which areas?
options: Only the method of self-harm
Social, peer group, education and home situations, caring responsibilities, social media/internet use, and any safeguarding issues
Only family psychiatric history
Only physical injuries
rationale: NG225 specifies that assessment of children and young people should additionally cover social, peer, education and home situations, caring responsibilities, social media/internet use, and child protection/safeguarding issues.
source: NICE - NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence

question: In the four-tier Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) model, Tier 4 refers to:
options: Universal services such as GPs and schools
Highly specialist services, including day and inpatient care
School counselling
Primary mental health workers
rationale: Tier 4 CAMHS covers highly specialist services such as inpatient and day-patient units for young people at greatest risk, needing intensive input.
source: NHS England - CAMHS Tier 4 service specification

question: In the four-tier CAMHS model, which tier describes universal services such as general practice, health visiting, school nursing and schools?
options: Tier 1
Tier 2
Tier 3
Tier 4
rationale: Tier 1 is universal services (GPs, school nursing, health visiting, schools) that promote mental wellbeing and identify early problems.
source: Open University OpenLearn - Introduction to adolescent mental health (CAMHS tiers)

scenario: A young person with a learning disability and autism is at risk of admission to a CAMHS Tier 4 inpatient unit.
question: What is the primary purpose of a Care, Education and Treatment Review (CETR)?
options: To decide the young person's school timetable
To ensure the young person is only admitted if absolutely necessary and for the minimum time, receiving the right care in the right place
To assess the parents' capacity
To calculate the cost of care
rationale: CETRs, part of NHS England's Transforming Care programme, aim to ensure admission only occurs when necessary and for the shortest time, with the young person receiving good care in the right place.
source: NHS England - Care, Education and Treatment Reviews

question: Care, Education and Treatment Reviews (CETRs) are aimed at which group of young people?
options: All young people admitted to any hospital
Young people with a learning disability and/or autism who are in, or at risk of admission to, a Tier 4 inpatient unit
Only young people detained under section 2
Young people with physical health conditions only
rationale: CETRs are for young people with learning disabilities and/or autism (and mental health needs) who are admitted to, or at risk of admission to, CAMHS Tier 4 inpatient units.
source: NHS England - Care, Education and Treatment Reviews

scenario: A 15-year-old assessed as Gillick competent consents to admission for mental health treatment, but her parents object.
question: Where a Gillick-competent under-16 gives valid consent to treatment or informal admission, what is the effect of parental objection?
options: Parental objection automatically blocks the treatment
The competent child's valid consent provides a lawful basis to proceed, so parental objection does not by itself prevent it
Treatment cannot proceed without both parents agreeing
The child must be detained under the Mental Health Act instead
rationale: A Gillick-competent child's valid consent provides lawful authority; a young person with capacity who consents to informal admission can be admitted irrespective of the views of a person with parental responsibility. (Refusal by a competent child raises separate, more complex issues.)
source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice - Chapter 19
